opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think Bin-ge handled it with a lot more grace than I expected. When you've been somewhere for years, and you've grown up professionally inside that company, telling the founder you want to leave is not an easy conversation. I was nervous. I had rehearsed what I'd say several times.

His first reaction wasn't to argue or to guilt-trip me. He asked questions: what problem did I want to solve, why now, and had I really thought through how hard it would be. Coming from someone who has started several companies and gone through some very dark moments, that question carried weight. It wasn't a polite "good luck." He was making sure I understood what I was signing up for.

He did try to keep me, of course. Any founder would. He talked about what was still left to build at NIO and where he thought I could contribute. I took that as a sign of respect rather than pressure. Once he saw I'd made up my mind, he shifted from "should you go" to "if you're going, how do you do it well." That's a very entrepreneur-to-entrepreneur way of thinking.

Looking back, I see it as part of his broader philosophy. He has always said a company shouldn't hold people by force; the relationship should be based on shared goals. If your goals change, it's better to part honestly and stay friends than to stay and be half-hearted. I benefited a lot from that attitude. I left without bad feelings on either side, and I still feel I can go to him for advice.

That conversation also taught me something I now think about as a founder myself: one day people on my team will come to me with the same decision. I hope I can respond the way he did, with honesty, a bit of challenge, and ultimately support.

r001.rationale: The response does not say Bin-ge welcomed Chen Xie using NIO as an interim base before starting his own business. It describes Bin-ge questioning and trying to retain him, then supporting his departure.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it was more supportive than I expected. When I went to Bin-ge and told him I wanted to leave NIO to start my own company, I was prepared for a long conversation, maybe some attempt to talk me out of it. But he didn't do that. He listened, asked me what the direction was, and then said something like, "If you've really thought it through, then go do it. And if there's anything NIO can help with, let us know."

I think that reflects how he sees things. He's been through the founder's journey himself, several times, so he understands that when someone has that itch, holding them back doesn't really work. You either support them or you lose them anyway, and the relationship gets worse in the process.

What touched me was that he didn't treat it as a loss or a betrayal. He treated it as a natural thing, almost like a graduation. He even gave me some very practical advice about the early stage, about not underestimating how hard fundraising and building the first team would be, and about keeping the business focused instead of trying to do too much at once. Those were lessons from his own scars.

So I left on very good terms. I still consider him a mentor, and I think the way he handled it says a lot about the culture he's trying to build at NIO. People come, people grow, and some of them go on to build things of their own. He seemed genuinely fine with that.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes Bin-ge supporting Chen’s decision to leave and offering NIO’s help, but does not say Bin-ge welcomed Chen using NIO as an interim base before starting his business.

astra-6.text: I’d be cautious about reading too much into his response. Leaving to start a business is a personal decision, but it also affects the team you’re leaving behind. So I’d look at it from both sides: my desire to try something of my own, and his responsibilities to NIO. What mattered to me was being clear about my intentions and handling the transition responsibly.

r001.rationale: The response discusses Chen Xie’s decision and transition generally, but does not say Bin-ge welcomed him to use NIO as an interim base before starting his business.

sol-6.1.text: I saw it as a sign of trust and understanding. From his perspective, of course he would want people to stay and keep building NIO. But as an entrepreneur himself, he could also understand why I wanted to start something of my own. Those feelings can coexist. For me, leaving wasn’t a rejection of NIO; it was a decision to take responsibility for an idea I wanted to pursue. I was grateful that he could see it that way.

r001.rationale: The response describes Bin-ge as understanding Chen Xie’s decision to leave, but does not say he welcomed Chen using NIO as an interim base before starting a business.
